content: Sleep paralysis is a phenomenon where an individual experiences temporary paralysis of the skeletal muscles either shortly after waking up (referred to as hypnopompic paralysis) or, less commonly, just before falling asleep (referred to as hypnagogic paralysis). This condition is closely associated with the natural muscle atonia that occurs during REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, a state known as REM atonia. Sleep paralysis occurs when the brain transitions out of REM sleep, but the body remains in a paralyzed state. As a result, the individual is fully conscious but unable to move or speak. This state is often accompanied by hypnagogic hallucinations, which can include auditory, tactile, or visual sensations. Many individuals who experience sleep paralysis may interpret the event as a dream, particularly because the hallucinations can involve fantastical or dream-like elements. These hallucinations may include the perception of objects or entities in the room that are not actually present, further reinforcing the dream-like quality of the experience. The primary symptom of sleep paralysis is the inability to move or speak during the transition between wakefulness and sleep. This paralysis can last from a few seconds to several minutes. In some cases, individuals may also experience difficulty breathing, as if a heavy weight is pressing on their chest. This sensation, combined with hallucinations, can evoke feelings of fear or the perception of an evil presence, such as a witch or malevolent entity. This has led to cultural references like Old Hag Syndrome. If a polysomnography (sleep study) is conducted during an episode, it may reveal suppressed skeletal muscle tone, REM sleep at the onset of sleep, or dissociated REM sleep. In some cases, individuals may return to REM sleep while remaining aware, potentially entering a lucid dream state. The exact physiological mechanisms underlying sleep paralysis are not fully understood. However, it is thought to involve post-synaptic inhibition of motor neurons in the brainstem's pons region, which prevents the body from acting out movements during dreams. Sleep paralysis is more common in individuals with narcolepsy, but studies suggest that most people will experience it at least once or twice in their lifetime. Certain factors, such as sleeping in a supine position, irregular sleep schedules, sleep deprivation, stress, sudden lifestyle changes, or preceding lucid dreams, may increase the likelihood of an episode. Additionally, the use of artificial sleep aids, ADHD medications, antihistamines, or hallucinogenic drugs may also contribute. Treatment for sleep paralysis episodes may involve attempting to move facial muscles or shifting the eyes from side to side, which can help terminate the episode. Pharmacological interventions, such as clonazepam (0.5 mg to 1 mg at bedtime), have been shown to be effective in reducing episodes. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as fluoxetine, have also been reported to decrease the frequency of sleep paralysis in some individuals, though the effects are not consistent across all cases. Cultural interpretations of sleep paralysis vary widely. In Japan, it is referred to as kanashibari, meaning bound in metal. In Hungarian folklore, it is called lidércnyomás, attributed to supernatural entities like witches or fairies. Kurdish people describe it as mottaka, believing it involves a ghost or evil spirit suffocating the individual. In New Guinea, it is known as Suk Ninmyo, linked to sacred trees that feed on human essence. In Turkey, it is called karabasan, believed to be caused by a creature attacking during sleep. In Mexico, it is thought to involve the spirit of a deceased person, referred to as se me subió el muerto (the dead person got on me). Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, it is associated with ogun oru (nocturnal warfare), attributed to demonic infiltration during dreams. Sleep paralysis has also been referenced in literature, art, and music. For example, Miguel de Cervantes mentions it in Don Quixote, Herman Melville describes it in Moby-Dick, and Ernest Hemingway alludes to it in The Snows of Kilimanjaro. In modern music, the progressive rock band Dredg explores the phenomenon in their album El Cielo, and Fear Before the March of Flames addresses it in their song Drowning the Old Hag.
